title: Explaining the magnitude of Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity via electron-electron exchange
authors: Bence Csakany, Alex J. W. Thom
abstract: Chiral molecular structure can couple to electron spin, leading to unexpected spin polarization effects. This Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS) was first reported for DNA molecules adsorbed on gold but its microscopic origin remains unclear. We demonstrated though simulation that the exchange arising from electron-electron Coulomb interactions within the self-consistent mean field (Hartree--Fock) approximation can yield significant ($\sim 2\%$) spin polarisation for $3$-methylcyclohexanone adsorbed on Cu(111) amplifying a much smaller ($\sim 0.0014\%$) initial bias, consistent with experiment. Symmetry considerations ensure the result is physically meaningful, while its ab-initio nature ensures all parameters are physically realistic. This amplification is connected to existing studies on spin-symmetry breaking in Hartree--Fock, providing a new pathway for understanding the magnitude of CISS as an emergent phenomenon of interacting electrons.
summary: The paper investigates Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS) using theoretical simulations on a molecule adsorbed on copper. It proposes that the magnitude of this spin polarization is not solely due to structural chirality or SOC, but rather emerges as an amplification effect driven by electron-electron exchange interactions within the Hartree-Fock framework. This offers a new physical pathway to explain observed spin phenomena in molecular junctions.
main_problem: The primary goal is to theoretically explain the magnitude of Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS), a spin polarization effect arising from molecular chirality, particularly when relativistic effects like SOC are weak.
main_result: The study demonstrates that electron-electron exchange interactions within the Hartree-Fock approximation can significantly amplify a small initial spin bias ($\sim 0.0014\%$) to yield a measurable spin polarization ($\sim 2\%$), providing a new mechanism for understanding CISS magnitude.
method: The research employs Non-Equilibrium Green's Functions (NEGF) formalism solved via Dyson equations, incorporating the Hartree-Fock approximation for electron interactions.
model_or_system: The model simulates a chiral molecule (3-methylcyclohexanone) adsorbed onto a metallic surface (Cu(111)), analyzed under conditions mimicking UV photoelectron spectroscopy.
key_observables: Spin polarization of photoelectrons, spin density difference resolved in different spatial directions (X, Y, Z), and the dependence of polarization on initial spin bias.
important_parameters: The calculation relies on setting parameters for leads ($\gamma_{bulk}, \gamma_{vacuum}, \gamma_{photoelectron}$) and simulating a specific incoming photon energy (210nm).
main_assumptions: Key approximations include using the Hartree-Fock method, employing the wide-band limit for lead self-energies, and assuming that electron-electron exchange is the dominant source of spin amplification.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic mechanism where small initial energy splits are amplified by exchange effects; subsequent figures show energy-resolved photoelectron spin polarization spectra comparing scenarios with and without bulk spin bias.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the CISS problem to setting up the NEGF framework using Dyson equations. It then analyzes how electron-electron exchange acts as an amplifier, culminating in quantitative results showing the magnitude of the effect.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses spin transport and correlation effects in nanoscale systems, which is highly relevant for understanding spintronics and molecular electronics where weak coupling to magnetic moments can be amplified by many-body interactions.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic diagram showing the change in en- ergy of each electron in a molecule due to an external influence. Each electron is in an approximate single particle state, a molecular orbital. The energy of these orbitals is per- turbed slightly by an external effect such as chiral phonons or spin-orbit coupling, along with breaking of time-reversal symmetry. Once the symmetry is broken, electron–electron exchange effects amplify the symmetry breaking leading to a much larger effect.

FIG. 2. Schematic of the Green’s-function mod- els used to study photoelectron transport through 3- methylcyclohexanone (3-MCHO) adsorbed on Cu(111). Top: ‘equilibrium’ setup comprising a semi-infinite bulk Cu lead coupled to the explicit Cu(111)+3-MCHO system. Bottom: ‘photoelectron’ setup, where additional photoelectron and vacuum leads are introduced to model excited-electron injec- tion and photoelectron emission, respectively. Shaded regions indicate occupied states below the corresponding Fermi lev- els.

FIG. 3. The photelectron (spin) density of the sys- tem. Left: The system of interest, 3-R-MCHO adsorbed into Cu(111). Middle: Photoelectron density (equation 17). Right: Photoelectron spin density resolved along the di- rection normal to the plane. Cyan/Orange is spin paral- lel/antiparallel to the surface normal respectively. The sur- face parallel components are zero, Figure SI-1.

FIG. 4. The magnitude and polarisation of the resul- tant photoelectrons. Left: Incoming photoelectron and outgoing (scattering) current. The variation in the current is due to the location of the virtual orbitals of the molecule. Most of the current does not make it across the interface. This is due to the limited delocalisation across the interface, as is typical for physisorbed molecules. The bulk copper was biased by 4% as described in the main text. Right: The spin polarisation of the resultant current. The bias creates an inherent 4% polarisation in the incoming electrons. The outgoing electrons do not have this and all variation is due to the spin-symmetry broken molecular orbitals....
